name: GFT: October Edition in Defence Colony
description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Defence Colony)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.1st October: Dolan SamantaTemple sculpture is usually read as devotion — divine bodies carved to be worshipped. This session argues it does something more: these images are sites where gender, desire, and authority are negotiated, not just depicted. Taking two ninth-to-eleventh-century carvings of Śiva and Pārvatī from the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at Kālañjara as its central text, and reading them through Puranic myth, Foucault, and Judith Butler's account of gender as performance, Dolan Samanta, a history educator and JNU-trained researcher, asks why Śiva appears nude, enraged, and armed, his sexuality fused with dominance, while Pārvatī appears smaller, modest, at once desired and desiring. The question stone carved a thousand years ago still puts to us: who was permitted power, and who was only expected to receive it?8th October: Tania KapoorMost parents still treat marks as the surest route to a child's future — but school mostly rewards memorising, following instructions, and reproducing the right answer in the right way, exactly the kind of work AI is fastest at absorbing. Tania Kapoor, a Delhi-based child and adolescent psychologist trained at AIIMS, argues that what will actually distinguish children going forward — adaptability, emotional regulation, impulse control, comfort with ambiguity — is precisely what classrooms and busy households keep treating as something to address "later" Grounded in clinical practice, this session asks what parents should be paying attention to now, before later becomes too late.15th October: Dr. Jasleen RanaEvery purchase carries a story that has little to do with the product itself — emotion, aspiration, insecurity, identity. Dr. Jasleen Rana, who holds a PhD in Consumer Psychology and teaches Marketing at JIMS Kalkaji, moves past the question of what we buy to the more revealing one why. Through brand archetypes, hidden motivations, and everyday examples — choosing one coffee shop over another, paying more for a brand that does exactly what a cheaper one does — this interactive session decodes the psychological triggers behind consumer choice, and what those choices reveal about identity, belonging, and self-image.22nd October: Shubham YadavWhat if ordinary citizens believed they had something to teach the members of the Constituent Assembly? Shubham Yadav, a Senior Research Fellow at JNU's Zakir Husain Centre for Educational Studies, argues that India's Constitution wasn't shaped by elites alone — it emerged from a running exchange in which both "the people" and "the makers" wanted to instruct each other on what the new nation should be. Framed as a conversation rather than a lecture, the session traces that two-way pedagogy, and what it reveals about how theConstitution actually came to be built.

name: #lecture: The Magic of Boredom
description: How do you get the ideas behind your short stories? Someone had asked the Russian writer Anton Chekhov. Reportedly, Chekhov had responded: “Put your cigarette on this ash-tray and I’ll write a story about it.”This response presents the perfect picture of modern literature that came into existence with the popularisation of print culture and the making of novels and short stories.Classical epics, oral tales, and myths and legends of the past took a great, telescopic view of grand subjects, particularly those of war and romance, in a world full of magic and fantasy populated by gods and kings.This lecture will show how modern literature, shaped by the rhythm of the factory, dominated by clock-time and full of industrial workers and a middle class, turned to everyday themes that resonated with ordinary people, and focused a microscopic lens on the small magic of the cigarette on the ash-tray.About the Speaker Saikat Majumdar is a novelist, critic and educator. He taught literature at Stanford University for nine years, has been a fellow at Wellesley College, the institutes of Advanced Study in JNU, Stellenbosch, Budapest, and Brasov, and is currently Professor of English & Creative Writing at Ashoka University.He is the author of five novels, most recently, The Remains of the Body, published as Penguin Random House’s 2024 Pride Month Selection. His other novels include The Scent of God (2019), a story of love between two teenage boys in a Hindu monastic boarding school, The Firebird (2015), which narrates a young boy’s destructive obsession with his mother’s life as an actress, and The Middle Finger (2022), a queer, contemporary college-campus retelling of the Ekalavya story.He has also published four books of nonfiction and criticism, including Open Intelligence: Education between Art and Artificial (2026), which outlines possibilities for education in the age of Artificial Intelligence with particular attention to the changing definitions of talent, merit, and career, The Amateur, a book about people who learned to read and write without proper educational support, and College: Pathways of Possibility (2018), a popular book on interdisciplinary liberal arts education in India.

name: Designing Your Life, The Stanford Way
description: About the LectureWhat if the life you're living right now is one you drifted into by default, not one you chose?We are born into stories, about success, work, money, relationships, identity and what a good life should look like. Somewhere along the way, those stories start to feel like our own, and a life shaped by default begins to feel like one shaped by choice.Stanford's Designing Your Life offers another way to look at it: life as something you can actively design. That doesn't mean finding one "true" self or one perfect path. It means moving towards self-authorship: questioning the narratives you inherited, imagining different futures, and accepting that there may be more than one life within you worth living.Design turns out to be an unusually useful lens for this, because it doesn't require you to know the answer before you begin. It lets you work with ambiguity, hold several possibilities at once, and experiment rather than predict. In a world where lives are increasingly nonlinear, that may be more useful than having a perfect plan.The session explores:How inherited social narratives quietly become the stories we live byWhy there may be more than one life within us worth livingHow designers work with ambiguity, and why that matters for life decisionsMoving from a life by default to a life by design: question, imagine, prototypeAbout the SpeakerNavyug Mohnot is a Stanford-certified Designing Your Life educator, coach and facilitator, a visiting faculty member at ISB and Ashoka University, and the founder and CEO of QAI Global. He is a certified leadership coach from Harvard University, has spoken at conferences around the world, and is a TEDx speaker ("Manifesting Desires, Embracing Contradictions"). He has coached professionals across the globe, served on company boards, and mentored startups as an angel investor. Navyug did his B.Tech at IIT Delhi and received the "Outstanding Contribution to National Development" award from the IIT Delhi Alumni Association. Outside work, he meditates, runs a film club, loves art, film and architecture, and hopes to direct a full-length film someday.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Clearing the Smoke and Mirrors
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that cuts through the winter blame game:Delhi blames Punjab, Punjab blames Delhi, and everyone blames the weather. So what is actually in the air we breathe?We've all been there: complaining about the AQI, feeling what the air does to our lungs, sleep, skin and routines. Every winter we're handed the same list of culprits: stubble burning, construction dust, industrial emissions, cars, trucks, garbage fires, landfills, brick kilns, diesel generators and, of course, the wind. The panels shout, the season passes, and by next November we're no clearer on which of these actually matters, or by how much.Atmospheric scientist Dr Mohammad Rafiuddin begins with Delhi's meteorology and geography: a landlocked city on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, hemmed in by the Himalayas, with winter air that sits still. It's a bad hand, but not a unique one, and if cities around the world with the same conditions have got their air under control, so can Delhi. From there, we'll go sector by sector through what's actually in the air, and which solutions would genuinely cut emissions from each.The session explores:Why Delhi's geography and winter weather trap pollution, and why that isn't an excuseWhat's actually in Delhi's air: transport, biomass and solid-fuel burning, waste, dust, construction, industry and stubbleWhich sources matter most, and by how muchThe solutions that would genuinely cut emissions, sector by sectorAbout the SpeakerDr Mohammad Rafiuddin is an atmospheric scientist who once built a fog-forecasting system for Bengaluru airport, which means pilots have landed on his maths. He holds a PhD in atmospheric sciences from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru, a Post Graduate Diploma in Urban Environmental Management and Law from National Law University, and a BTech in mechanical engineering from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Hyderabad.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Can We Make Delhi a Human City?
description: Welcome to Human City Conversations where we have intimate conversations about how cities are built, how they are lived, and who gets to shape them.Conversation 1: HOW DO WE MAKE DELHI A HUMAN CITY?Delhi is a city of contradictions. It has some of India's best public institutions, an expanding metro network, enormous infrastructure projects and a new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 that sets out a vision for how the city should grow and change over the next two decades. And yet, the experience of living in Delhi can be very different.Millions of people spend hours commuting across the city. Walking can feel like an afterthought. Public spaces are often unevenly distributed and poorly connected. For many women, moving through the city comes with a calculation of safety that men may never have to make. And then there is the air. Every winter, Delhi's air pollution becomes a public health crisis forcing a city of millions to think about something as fundamental as whether it is safe to breathe outside.So how can a city with so much planning, infrastructure and investment still struggle with some of the most basic conditions of everyday urban life? Perhaps the problem is not simply how much we build, perhaps we need to ask a more fundamental question:What kind of city are we actually trying to build? And more importantly, who is that city being built for?For the first Human City Conversation, urbanist Jagan Shah joins Ruchita Bansal for an open conversation about Delhi, its future and the gap between the city we plan on paper and the city people actually experience. We'll explore what makes a city genuinely liveable from mobility and housing to public space, safety, air pollution and neighbourhoods and look at what Delhi's new Master Plan for 2047 could mean on the ground.What to ExpectA curated, open conversation between urbanist Jagan Shah and Ruchita BansalA look at Delhi's urban future and what the new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 could mean on the groundA discussion about the gap between the city we plan and the city people actually experienceA closer look at how cities are shaped by policies, infrastructure and development decisionsPerspectives on what makes a city genuinely liveable, accessible and inclusiveA 30 minute Q&A SessionInformal discussion and one on one conversation after the conversationEvent Details📅 Sunday, 11 October 2026🕔 5:00 PM onwards📍 Kunzum Books, GK II, Delhi☕ Your ticket includes one coffee/tea .About the SpeakerJagan Shah is an urbanist, architect and former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), with decades of experience working at the intersection of urban planning, policy, governance and development. He has been closely involved in shaping India's urban policy and planning landscape, including work connected to Delhi's Master Plan, the Smart Cities Mission and other national urban development programmes. His work has involved developing and implementing policies and frameworks that influence how Indian cities grow, transform and respond to the challenges of rapid urbanisation.Over the years, Jagan has worked across urban planning, housing, infrastructure, heritage, governance and institutional development, working with governments and institutions at different levels.His experience spans both the making of plans and policies and the realities of implementing them, making him particularly well placed to examine the gap between the city we envision on paper and the city that people actually experience.About the ModeratorRuchita Bansal is an architect and urban planner with 15 years of experience working on cities, urban development and planning policy. Her work has ranged from developing planning frameworks and regulations to working directly on large-scale urban transformation projects. She was part of the team behind Ayodhya Vision 2047, working on one of India's most complex and rapidly transforming urban environments and seeing first-hand the challenges of translating ambitious plans and visions into reality on the ground.Today, Ruchita is the Creator and Host of The Human City Podcast and the founder of SheCity India, using conversations, research and storytelling to make urban planning more accessible and bring the discussion about cities beyond the professional planning community. Through The Human City, she explores a simple but often overlooked question: what does all this planning mean for the people who actually live in our cities?Note: Attendance implies consent to being filmed for event documentation. If you do not wish to be filmed, please reach out to your curator for the evening, Ruchita. Come curious. Come questioning. Come ready to talk about the city we call home.

name: GFT: October Edition in Janpath
description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Janpath)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.6th October: Harshit BishtYour phone finishes your sentences, your inbox drafts your replies, a chatbot will happily name your business for you — and it's doing the same for millions of other people at once. Harshit Bisht, a PhD scholar in artificial intelligence at IIT Delhi researching multimodal foundation models for scientific discovery, asks what happens when systems trained on existing culture start setting the default for what counts as a "good" or "natural" answer, across countries, languages, and ways of seeing the world. Built around everyday experience rather than technical background, the session isn't trying to settle whether AI is good or bad — only what happens to the differences between us as these tools get better at helping each of us individually.13th October: Prerna VatsWords like "comprehensive," "flexible," and "excellence" fill education policy documents, but what do they mean once they reach an actual classroom — and who decides? Prerna Vats, a PhD scholar in Women and Gender Studies at Ambedkar University and a teacher trainer and sexuality educator, reads the National Education Policy 2020 alongside Krishna Kumar's 1992 text What Is Worth Teaching to trace the gap between education's imagined goals and its measurable outcomes. The session puts the figure of the teacher — and participants' own educational journeys — at the centre, asking who gets left out in the pursuit of "quality" education.27th October: Abhishek PanchalClimate communication has leaned so heavily on doomsday narratives that it often produces disengagement instead of action, while pseudo-sustainable habits let people feel involved without shifting the underlying politics. Abhishek Panchal, a research scientist at Ashoka University and former ISRO scientist-engineer, introduces Pralay, a cooperative strategy board game where players navigate competing climate priorities at the individual, state, and global level. Built on storytelling and discussion rather than lecture, the session asks whether an evening around a game table can do what doomsday statistics haven't — and examines whether it actually shifts attitudes, not just conversation.

name: Tughlaqabad: Rise and Fall of a Dynasty
description: Rising dramatically from the rocky landscape of southern Delhi, Tughlaqabad stands as one of the most ambitious and haunting experiments in medieval urban history. Built in the fourteenth century by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, the vast fortified city marked the beginning of the Tughlaq dynasty and reflected a new architectural language defined by massive walls, sloping fortifications and an imposing sense of military power. Yet the city that was conceived to embody permanence would itself become closely associated with decline and abandonment.This walk explores the rise and fall of the Tughlaq dynasty through the extraordinary remains of Tughlaqabad and its surrounding landscape. Participants trace the vision behind this ambitious capital while uncovering the stories of Adilabad Fort, Nai ka Kot and the political and architectural developments that shaped the dynasty's early years. The experience culminates at the tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, one of the earliest and most distinctive monuments of Tughlaq architecture, where its design is explored in connection with the earlier tomb of Zafar Khan and the architectural ideas that preceded the Tughlaqs.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Tughlaqabad and the emergence of the Tughlaq dynasty in fourteenth-century Delhi.Explore Tughlaqabad Fort and understand Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's extraordinary vision of creating a vast fortified capital.Examine the distinctive military architecture of the fort, including its massive defensive walls, sloping bastions and strategic relationship with the surrounding rocky landscape.Discuss the rise of the Tughlaq dynasty and the circumstances that eventually contributed to the decline and abandonment of this ambitious imperial city.Explore the story and significance of Adilabad Fort and understand its relationship with the larger fortified landscape of Tughlaqabad.Discuss Nai ka Kot and its place within the wider story of Delhi's medieval defensive and urban landscape.Visit the tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and examine one of the earliest examples of the architectural style that would come to define the Tughlaq period.Compare its architectural ideas with the earlier tomb of Zafar Khan, exploring the transition in tomb architecture and the developments that preceded the distinctive Tughlaq style.Conclude with a discussion on the ambitions, achievements and eventual decline of the Tughlaq dynasty, and how Tughlaqabad continues to preserve the memory of one of medieval Delhi's most dramatic experiments in imperial city-building.Key Themes & Highlights Rise of the Tughlaq DynastyTughlaqabad FortMedieval military architectureRise and fall of an imperial capitalAdilabad FortNai ka KotGhiyasuddin Tughlaq's TombEvolution of Tughlaq architectureConnection with Zafar Khan's TombDelhi Sultanate politics and power

name: Delhi Ridge: From Empires to the Uprising
description: Long before Delhi expanded into the metropolis we know today, a rocky ridge defined its geography, protected its settlements, and silently witnessed the rise and fall of empires. Delhi Ridge: From Empires to the Uprising explores this remarkable landscape where natural history and human history have remained inseparable for more than two thousand years. Despite his young age, he has participated in and won several state-level music competitions and is also a Sangam Kala Group winner.His soulful and soothing voice has earned him appreciation and blessings from renowned personalities of the ghazal and music fraternity, including Ustaad Ghulam Ali Khan Sahib and Murshid Ali. His musical journey is deeply rooted in the guidance of his guru, Sh. Sudhanshu Ehsaas, who has been nurturing and training him since Yashraj was just six years old.The talent that Yashraj displays today is the result of years of dedicated riyaaz, discipline, learning and hard work—both by the young artist and his guru. His understanding of music, command over ghazal and Sufi compositions, and his naturally peaceful and expressive voice make him a truly promising young performer. Depot 48 provide talented singers and performers with a platform where they can build their artistic profile, gain confidence and, most importantly, experience the energy and dynamics of a live audience.For Yashraj, this opportunity is especially meaningful. At just 12, he already possesses the musical ability of a seasoned young artist, while live audience engagement is naturally an area where he will continue to grow with experience. With more stage exposure, interactions with diverse audiences and continued riyaaz, he has immense potential to develop into a confident and compelling live performer.

description: There are times in history that ask something different of us.
